say: Today you become pattern generalisers. That is a big word for a simple, powerful idea: if you can see HOW a pattern grows, you can jump straight to the 100th figure without drawing 100 pictures.
Mathematicians and coders do this all the time. By the end of today you will say the rule for any figure in words, and use it backwards too.
I have a secret machine. It does two things to every number. You call out a number, I tell you what comes out.
When you think you know the rule, do not shout it. Test it on the next number first. Then say it in words.
If all 8 of us high-five everyone else once, how many high fives is that? Write your guess in the corner of your whiteboard. Is it more or less than 50?
Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks, and before you touch the objects. Silent thinking. I will show the clock. Then talk with your partner.
stuck: Stuck: start with 2 children. Then 3. Draw each child as a dot and each high five as a line.
Stuck on the table: when a new child joins, how many NEW high fives does that child make?
If a pair wants more: how many high fives for a class of 30? Is there a quick way without adding 29 numbers?

say: “Squares in a row. Figure 1 has 4 sticks, figure 2 has 7, figure 3 has 10. Each new square adds 3, not 4, because it shares a side with the square before. So I start with 1 stick and add 3 for every square: sticks = 3 × figure number + 1.”
“For figure 25 I do not draw 25 squares. 3 × 25 + 1 = 76. And backwards: 61 sticks. Undo the last step first: 61 − 1 = 60, then 60 ÷ 3 = 20. Figure 20. I check: 3 × 20 + 1 = 61.”

“Supposition. 24 vehicles with 70 wheels. Suppose they are ALL motorcycles: 48 wheels. I am 22 wheels short. Each time a motorcycle becomes a car I get 2 more wheels, so 22 ÷ 2 = 11 cars. Check both facts: 11 + 13 = 24 vehicles and 44 + 26 = 70 wheels.”

do: Ask: “What does each new figure add? Show me where it is in the picture.”
Ask: “Say your rule in words. Does it work for figure 1, 2 AND 3?”
Ask: “What did you suppose? How much does the total change for each swap?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Make a table: figure number in one row, count in the other.”
Hint 2: “Colour the part that stays the same in one colour and the part that grows in another.”
Hint 3: “To go backwards, undo the steps in reverse order: take away first, then divide.”

say: “Mei says 10 squares in a row need 31 sticks, so 20 squares need 62. Is she right?”
“In Q4 and Q5, which did you like better: a guess-and-check table or supposition? Why?”
ask: “Mei says 10 squares in a row need 31 sticks, so 20 squares need 62. Is she right?”

Mei is not right: 20 squares need 3 × 20 + 1 = 61 sticks. The rule is “3 for each square, plus 1 starting stick”. Doubling 31 doubles the starting stick too, so it counts one stick too many. The same thing happens with the end chairs in Q1.

say: “Today you found how patterns grow, said the rule in words, used it forwards and backwards, and solved two-kinds problems by supposing. That is generalising: one rule for every case.”
“Do the exit ticket on your own, then show me.”

p5l9-title.note: Minutes 0 to 2 (opening, inside the 90-minute clock). Objective: Continue growing patterns drawn as figures, say the rule for any figure in words (for example, sticks = 3 × figure number + 1) and explain it from the picture, work backwards from a total to find the figure, and solve "two kinds of things" problems with a guess-and-check table and with supposition. Thinking strategies today: LOOK FOR A PATTERN, MAKE A TABLE, WORK BACKWARDS, GUESS AND CHECK, SUPPOSITION. Materials: matchsticks or toothpicks (about 40), square paper tiles or the square grid from the cut-out pages, mini whiteboards, workbook. Online: children have toothpicks and paper squares ready on the desk and build each figure on camera; pairs go to breakout rooms for the explore and page 1 and check their tables against the slide. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson; every lesson adds up to 90): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6.5 (one check for both puzzles, no volunteer round, nobody is marked), warm-up 6.5 to 12 (one game round, four quick questions), explore 12 to 25.5 (pair work 5.5 minutes at most, then two questions together; a Go further what-if is on the explore slide for any pair that finishes), teaching 25.5 to 37 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 37 to 41, workbook page 1 41 to 55 (the questions without a star; after question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder), check together 55 to 59, short teaching before page 2 59 to 62.5, workbook page 2 62.5 to 71.5 (alone: start with the questions named at the top, then choose; starred parts are take-home; nobody has to finish), check together 71.5 to 74.5, talk time 74.5 to 80 (you may say pass; volunteers first; the first step of the Investigation is take-home), exit ticket 80 to 85.5, reflection 85.5 to 88 (pass is always OK), stamp typed in the chat and goodbye 88 to 89, and the buffer 89 to 90 (floating time: spend it first if you run late, never fill it on purpose). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child and have no clock time. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and never splits a pair unless both children agree. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." SPINE: Today's tool is Try something simpler. Solve 1, 2, 3 cases first, find how the answer grows, then handle the real size. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p5l9-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6.5. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Show puzzle 1 and give about a minute; click to show the short answer later. Then show puzzle 2 and give about a minute. Open with one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, drawing or counting, so everyone can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. ONE check for both puzzles: after puzzle 2, everyone says the answers together on three (face to face, you may glance at papers held low as you walk round; online, nothing is held up to the camera). Then click through the two short answers and say each with one short reason. NO volunteer round here (volunteers come in the talk time). Never boards in front of the group, never read out answers with names, no tally, no ranking. Never record scores. Answers and what to listen for. Q1: 9 sticks. Each new triangle shares a side with the one before, so it adds 2 sticks.; Q2: 21 sticks for 10 triangles (3 + 9 × 2, or 2 × 10 + 1). 41 sticks make 20 triangles (take away the 1 extra stick, then 40 ÷ 2). Continuing the list also works. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES (about 4.5 minutes). Show the two puzzles one at a time. Say one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is one that any child can try with objects, drawing or counting, so everybody can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Answers are shown PRIVATELY, never on boards in front of the group. Face to face: children write on their own paper and show it only to you as you walk round. Online: children say the answers together on three; nothing is held up to the camera. Do not read answers out with names, do not keep a tally, do not rank. Use ONE check for both puzzles (after puzzle 2, everyone says the answers together on three), then click through the answers and say each one with one short reason. There is NO volunteer round in the sneak-peek; volunteers come in the talk time. Never choose a child because you saw a wrong answer. Never record scores. Choosing a start: every child has the same neutral line on workbook page 1: "After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (The number is the last question on page 1 of this lesson.) Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never single out a child by name and never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless BOTH children agree. Any child may swap at any time.

p5l9-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 9. Guess My Rule. Play without the slide first if you like: children call a number, you answer from your secret rule (times 3, then add 1), and write the pairs on the board. Play ONE round only, using the slide: click to show 2 to 7, 5 to 16, 10 to 31. Ask: "Is it add 5? 2 + 5 = 7 works! Now test 5." (5 + 5 = 10, not 16). This is the habit for today: TEST your rule on every case, not just the first. Then: "Say it in words: multiply by 3, then add 1." Click to reveal. Listen for children who say "it goes up by 3" (true for the steps) but cannot say what happens to 100. That gap is today's lesson.

p5l9-warm2.note: Minutes 9 to 12. Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. Ask after 1: "What is the rule? add 4." After 2: "What do you notice about 1, 4, 9, 16, 25?" (square numbers: 1 × 1, 2 × 2 ...). After 3: "multiply by 3 each time", so it is not the same kind of pattern as 1. After 4: the 20th even number is 2 × 20 = 40, a rule in words: 2 × the place. Answers: 23 and 27; 36; 162; 40. If you are short of time, skip question 4.

p5l9-explore1.note: Minutes 12 to 25.5 (the whole explore; this slide 12 to 21.5). Pairs. Online: breakout rooms, each pair draws dots on a whiteboard and joins them. Predict first: most children guess 8 × 8 = 64 or 8 + 7; write guesses down. Let them draw 2, 3, 4 and 5 dots before they look for the pattern. Pair work is at most 5.5 minutes: stop the table at 6 children (the quick rule for 8 and for 30 children is the Go further what-if). Anyone who wants more (open to every pair): a class of 8 or of 30. The picture shows 1, 3 and 6 lines for 2, 3 and 4 children. PROTECTED THINK TIME: before the pairs touch anything, say "Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks" and show the clock; then pairs talk and start. PAIR WORK IS CAPPED AT 5.5 MINUTES: say "Pencils down" at minute 21.5 and bring the group back (the minutes before that include the 30 seconds of thinking, finding materials and, in lessons that use them, the move to and from breakout rooms). GO FURTHER (say it as soon as a pair has finished the task): any pair that finishes early may try the what-if question on the next slide. It is open to every pair, not a reward. Answer: 8 children: 28. 30 children: 435. 12 children: 66. With n children each high-fives (n − 1) others, but every high five is counted twice, so the number is n × (n − 1) ÷ 2. For 12 children: 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66. The table 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21 … also works.

p5l9-explore2.note: Minutes 21.5 to 25.5. Pencils down: gather the pairs. Answers: 1) 5 children: 10. 6 children: 15. 2) Table 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 children: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. The jumps are 2, 3, 4, 5: a new child high-fives everyone already there, so the 4th child adds 3, the 5th adds 4 and so on (the 6th child adds 5). Go further what-if, not asked together: 8 children 28, and 30 children: each high-fives 29 others, 30 × 29 = 870, but every high five is counted twice (once by each child), so 870 ÷ 2 = 435. Do not push for this if nobody finds it; it returns on the Go further page. Note the jumps 2, 3, 4, 5 … grow each time; today we mostly study patterns that grow by the SAME amount each time. TWO questions together only (about a minute each), then move on. GO FURTHER what-if (open to every pair as soon as it has finished; nobody waits): 8 children: 28. 30 children: 435. 12 children: 66. With n children each high-fives (n − 1) others, but every high five is counted twice, so the number is n × (n − 1) ÷ 2. For 12 children: 12 × 11 ÷ 2 = 66. The table 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21 … also works.

p5l9-teach1.note: Minutes 25.5 to 27.5. Teach. Children build the three figures with toothpicks. Ask first: "How many sticks in figure 4? Figure 25?" Click the table row. Look at the picture: the teal sticks are the 3 new ones each time. Think-aloud: "Figure 2 is not 2 times figure 1 (8): the middle side is shared, so we save a stick. Each new square adds 3. I start with 1 stick and add 3 for each square: 3 times the figure number, plus the 1 extra." Then check the rule on three figures, not one. Trap to name: 25 lots of 3 plus 4 would be 79 (wrong), because the first square already counts its 4 sticks. The rule 3 × 25 + 1 = 76 is safe.

p5l9-try1.note: Minutes 27.5 to 29. Whiteboards, then click. a) 12 − 7 = 5. b) Figure 1 has 7 = 5 × 1 + 2, figure 2 has 12 = 5 × 2 + 2: dots = 5 × figure number + 2. Figure 12: 60 + 2 = 62. (Two items only.)

p5l9-we1.note: Minutes 29 to 31.5. Worked example: backwards. Children first say what the machine does going forwards: times 3, then plus 1. Going backwards we undo in reverse order: the last step first. Click step 1, then step 2. Always check by going forward again. Ask: "What if the answer was 62 sticks?" (62 − 1 = 61, 61 ÷ 3 is not whole, so no figure uses exactly 62 sticks.) This is Q1c and Q3c on the worksheet.

p5l9-try2.note: Minutes 31.5 to 33. Whiteboards. a) 100 − 1 = 99, 99 ÷ 3 = 33. b) 50 − 1 = 49, 49 ÷ 3 is not a whole number. (Two items only.)

p5l9-we2.note: Minutes 33 to 35.5. Worked example: two ways to see one pattern. First let children count the grey tiles in figures 1, 2 and 3 on their own. Then show Way 1 (top and bottom rows plus the two end tiles): figure 12 has 14 + 14 + 2 = 30 grey tiles. Way 2: the whole 3 by 14 rectangle has 42 tiles; 12 are yellow, so 42 − 12 = 30. Both rules are the same: 3 × (figure + 2) − figure = 2 × figure + 6. Do not need to simplify with letters; just check that both give 8, 10, 12 for the first three figures. The grey count grows by 2 each time, which is why the rule has 2 × figure number in it, like the chairs in Q1.

p5l9-key.note: Minutes 35.5 to 37. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Doubling: figure 20 is NOT twice figure 10, because the starting stick or the end chairs get counted twice. (2) Counting the jumps wrongly, 25 lots of 3 instead of 24 for figure 25 when starting from figure 1, or writing the rule as "add 3" without saying what to do with the figure number. (3) Supposition: dividing the gap by the value of one thing (22 ÷ 4) instead of the change for each swap (22 ÷ 2), and not checking BOTH facts (how many things and the total).

p5l9-break.note: Minutes 37 to 41. 4 minutes. Online: everyone stands on camera. Do the pattern for 12 moves (children say the number of each move). Then ask: what is the 20th move? The 30th? (every 3rd move is a stamp, so multiples of 3: 30th is a stamp, 20th is a clap since 20 = 18 + 2.) Do not let children count up to 30; ask for a rule.

p5l9-ws1.note: Minutes 41 to 55. Walk around. Ask "Show me where in the picture the rule comes from" before any help. Q1 (c) (d) and Q2 (c) are take-home (starred); do not wait for them. Anyone who wants more (open to every pair): draw figure 4 of the border-tiles pattern from the slides and count the grey tiles (12 grey). Everyone sees the same neutral line: "After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (Question 2 is the last question to do in class on page 1 of this lesson.) Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless BOTH children agree. Think harder is the next pages after the Investigation page in the workbook. IN CLASS NOW: Q1 (a) (b) and Q2 (a) (b). Parts marked with a star in the workbook are take-home: say so once ("the starred parts are for home") and do not wait for them.

p5l9-ws1ans.note: Minutes 55 to 59. One pair explains Q1 (a) (b); click through the rest (Q1 (c) (d) and Q2 (c) are take-home, their answers are here for you). Click each answer after a pair explains. Q1c: 50 − 2 = 48, 48 ÷ 2 = 24. Q1d: 2 × 20 + 2 = 42; doubling counts the two end chairs twice. Q2a: the first house needs 6 sticks; each new house shares its left wall, so it needs a roof (2), a floor (1), a top (1) and a right wall (1) = 5. Q2c: 200 − 1 = 199, 199 ÷ 5 = 39 remainder 4. Compare with the border-tiles example on the slides: the grey tiles grow by 2 each figure, so the rule has 2 × figure number in it.

p5l9-teachgs.note: Minutes 59 to 61. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q3). Start with a guess that is easy to check: half and half, 6 and 6 = $30. Too much by $1. Ask: "Which way do we change it?" A teh costs less, so we need more teh and fewer kopi. Each swap (one kopi becomes one teh) takes $1 off. One swap: 7 teh, 5 kopi = $29. Compare a random guess of 2 and 10 (way too much): a table that you CHANGE using what the last row told you finds the answer in 3 or 4 rows. Always check both facts: number of drinks AND the total.

p5l9-teachsup.note: Minutes 61 to 62.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4). The same problem as the table, but faster. Click through. The key question after step 2 is "what happens to the total when I change ONE motorcycle into ONE car?" The answer is 2, not 4 (the motorcycle's 2 wheels are replaced). Show the other way too: suppose all cars: 96 wheels, 26 too many, each swap removes 2, 13 motorcycles. Same answer. Compare with the table: when numbers are big, supposition is quicker.

p5l9-ws2.note: Minutes 62.5 to 71.5. Children work alone. Q3 and Q4 (a) are in class; Q4 (b) and Q5 are take-home (starred). Q3: check that each row changes from the one before. Q5b: a good explanation says that each wrong answer costs 7 marks, so scores go down in 7s from 100. Page 2 is a menu, not a wall. Everyone sees the same line: start with Q3 and Q4 (a), then choose. Nobody has to finish; stop at minute 71.5 whatever has been done, because the check-together slide gives every answer with its explanation. Starred parts are take-home (their answers are on the check slide for you; do not spend class time on them). Walk round, ask "what could you try first?", and give the first hint before any answer.

p5l9-ws2ans.note: Minutes 71.5 to 74.5. One child explains Q3; click through the rest (Q4 (b) and Q5 are take-home, their answers are here for you). Click after a child explains. Q3: 15 × $7 = $105 if all child; $145 − $105 = $40; each adult in place of a child adds $5; 40 ÷ 5 = 8 adults. Q4: 30 × 20¢ = $6.00; $10.20 − $6.00 = $4.20; each swap adds 30¢; $4.20 ÷ 30¢ = 14. Check 14 × 50¢ = $7.00 and 16 × 20¢ = $3.20, total $10.20. Q5a: all correct is 100; each wrong costs 5 + 2 = 7; 100 − 65 = 35; 35 ÷ 7 = 5 wrong; 15 correct; check 75 − 10 = 65. Q5b: 100 − 80 = 20, which is not a multiple of 7, so no whole number of wrong answers fits.

p5l9-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) Red (50 = 8 × 6 + 2, so it is the 2nd bead of a group). 49 yellow beads: 16 full groups of 6 give 96 beads and 48 yellow, and beads 97 to 100 are red, red, blue, yellow. A2) 96 (each row of 5 seats 12, and 8 × 12 = 96). One long row seats only 82. Splitting the tables gives more end seats. A3) 12 goats and 23 chickens (all chickens would have 70 legs; 24 legs short; each goat adds 2 legs). Check: 48 + 46 = 94. A4) 4, 9, 16: square numbers. The first 20 odd numbers add up to 20 × 20 = 400. (Each new odd number adds an L-shaped layer to a square of dots.)

p5l9-gofurther.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 61. The counts go 1, 5, 13, 25, 41, 61 (add 4, 8, 12, 16, 20). Or: each diamond is two square numbers of dots, 6 × 6 + 5 × 5 = 36 + 25 = 61. B2) 18. She answered 22 questions. All 22 correct would be 88 marks; each wrong answer costs 4 + 1 = 5 marks; 88 − 68 = 20, 20 ÷ 5 = 4 wrong. Check: 72 − 4 = 68. B3) 5. The numbers 1 to 9 use 9 digits. That leaves 91 digits: 45 two-digit numbers (10 to 54) use 90 of them, so the 100th digit is the first digit of 55. Make up your own (printed under Go further): Make up a growing pattern with dots or matchsticks. Draw figures 1, 2 and 3, and ask a partner for figure 10. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l9-gofurther2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 61. The counts go 1, 5, 13, 25, 41, 61 (add 4, 8, 12, 16, 20). Or: each diamond is two square numbers of dots, 6 × 6 + 5 × 5 = 36 + 25 = 61. B2) 18. She answered 22 questions. All 22 correct would be 88 marks; each wrong answer costs 4 + 1 = 5 marks; 88 − 68 = 20, 20 ÷ 5 = 4 wrong. Check: 72 − 4 = 68. B3) 5. The numbers 1 to 9 use 9 digits. That leaves 91 digits: 45 two-digit numbers (10 to 54) use 90 of them, so the 100th digit is the first digit of 55. Make up your own (printed under Go further): Make up a growing pattern with dots or matchsticks. Draw figures 1, 2 and 3, and ask a partner for figure 10. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l9-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then the "see it" slide, then the walk-through. These are Go further Q5 and Q6 (the first two of the three Go further items). Answers: 1) 61 dots. 2) 18 correct.

p5l9-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answers. Ask: What do you notice about the rows of the diamond? Do the blanks count as answered? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p5l9-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. E1: in a diamond the rows go up 1, 3, 5 … to the widest row and back down. The widest row of figure 6 has 2 × 6 − 1 = 11 dots. The top half, including the widest row, is a square number of dots (6 × 6 = 36 for figure 6) and the bottom half is the square number before it (5 × 5 = 25). Figure 6: 36 + 25 = 61. B2: blank questions score nothing and lose nothing, so only the 22 answered ones matter: suppose all 22 correct (88 marks), the gap is 20, each wrong answer costs 5 (the 4 you do not get and the 1 taken away), so 4 wrong and 18 correct.

p5l9-gap-last.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM last (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Last digits of products"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Spot the pattern. SAY: Only the last digit matters, so keep only the last digit each time. Write the last digit after 1 seven, 2 sevens, 3 sevens, 4 sevens, and carry on. ASK: When does the list of last digits start to repeat? How long is the cycle, and where does 30 land in it? LISTEN FOR: Sevens: 7, 9, 3, 1, then repeats (cycle of 4). 30 = 7 x 4 + 2, so the 2nd in the cycle: 9. Fours: 4, 6, 4, 6 (cycle of 2); 25 is odd, so 4. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) 9. (b) 4. WHY: Last digits of 7, 7x7, ... are 7, 9, 3, 1, 7, 9, 3, 1, ... 30 mod 4 = 2, so the last digit is 9. Fours: 4, 6, 4, 6, ... 25 is an odd position, so 4. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): Multiply 2 by itself 22 times. What is the last digit? Answer: 4 (the cycle is 2, 4, 8, 6 and 22 mod 4 = 2).

p5l9-gap-range.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM range (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Multiples in a range"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Try something simpler. SAY: Try something simpler first: how many multiples of 7 are there up to 100? Then up to 500? What do you do with the two answers? ASK: Is 100 a multiple of 7? Is 500? Why does that matter? What number do you test for "multiple of 7 and of 2"? LISTEN FOR: 500 / 7 = 71 remainder 3 gives 71 multiples up to 500; 100 / 7 = 14 remainder 2 gives 14 up to 100. 71 - 14 = 57. In (b) in the 2 table and the 7 table means in the 14 table: 500 / 14 = 35, 100 / 14 = 7, 35 - 7 = 28. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) 57 multiples of 7. (b) 28 multiples of 14. WHY: Multiples of 7 up to 500: 71. Up to 100: 14. Neither 100 nor 500 is a multiple of 7, so 71 - 14 = 57. Multiples of 14 up to 500: 35, up to 100: 7, so 28. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): How many multiples of 9 are between 200 and 700? Answer: 55.

p5l9-gap-gaps.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM gaps (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "The gap of the gaps"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Make a table. SAY: Make a table with 3 columns: the tower number, the blocks, and the gap. Then add a fourth column for the gap of the gaps. ASK: What is the gap going to be between Tower 5 and Tower 6? Between Tower 9 and Tower 10? LISTEN FOR: Gaps 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17. Listen for a table that keeps the pattern going row by row. Early finishers may notice each tower is a square number plus 2. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) The gaps are 1, 3, 5, 7. They go up by 2 each time. (b) 51 blocks. (c) 83 blocks. WHY: Tower 6: 18 + 9 = 27. Tower 7: 27 + 11 = 38. Tower 8: 38 + 13 = 51. Tower 9: 51 + 15 = 66. Tower 10: 66 + 17 = 83. Pattern check: Tower n has (n - 1) x (n - 1) + 2 blocks, so Tower 10 is 9 x 9 + 2 = 83. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): Tower 1 has 1 block, Tower 2 has 2, Tower 3 has 5, Tower 4 has 10. The gaps go up by 2 each time. How many blocks in Tower 7? Answer: 37.

p5l9-gap-woven.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM woven (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Two sequences woven together"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Spot the pattern. SAY: Look at every other number. Underline the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th. Then underline the 2nd, 4th, 6th. What is each list doing? ASK: Which list does the 15th number belong to? How many steps from the first number of that list is it? LISTEN FOR: Odd places: 3, 7, 11, 15 (add 4). Even places: 50, 46, 42 (take away 4). 15th is the 8th odd-place number: 3 + 7 x 4 = 31. 16th is the 8th even-place number: 50 - 7 x 4 = 22. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) 38 and 19. (b) 31. (c) 22. WHY: Odd places go up by 4: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, ... so the 15th number (the 8th odd-place number) is 3 + 4 x 7 = 31. Even places go down by 4: 50, 46, 42, 38, ... so the 16th number (the 8th even-place number) is 50 - 4 x 7 = 22. The list continues 15, 38, 19, 34, ... so the next two numbers are 38 and 19. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): Siti writes: 5, 80, 9, 74, 13, 68, ... Find the 12th number. Answer: 50.

p5l9-gap-op.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM op (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "A rule from examples"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Make a table. SAY: Make a table of the pairs. Look at what happens to the first number in each example. Try a rule, then test it on all four. ASK: Does your rule work for all four examples? Why is one example not enough? LISTEN FOR: Rule: first number x (second number + 1). Listen for children testing a guess on every example and dropping it if it fails (Guess and check inside the table). Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) 30. (b) 7. WHY: The rule is a x (b + 1): 2 x 4 = 8, 4 x 2 = 8, 5 x 3 = 15, 3 x 4 = 12. So 6 x 5 = 30. For x ★ 3: x times 4 = 28, so x = 7. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): A new machine: 1 ● 4 = 7, 2 ● 5 = 11, 3 ● 2 = 11, 5 ● 1 = 16. Find 4 ● 6. Answer: 18 (the rule is 3 x the first number + the second number).

p5l9-talk.note: Minutes 74.5 to 80. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: no, 20 squares need 3 × 20 + 1 = 61 sticks. Doubling doubles the 1 extra starting stick too, so it is one stick too many. Draw 10 squares, then another 10 squares joined on: the 11th square joins the 10th by sharing a side, so the sticks add up to 31 + 30 = 61. The same trap appears with chairs in Q1d. Second question if time: "In Q4 and Q5, which method did you like better, a table or supposing? Why?" Protected think time: before anyone speaks, everyone thinks silently for 30 seconds (show the clock). Then pairs talk. This applies to the explore, to the talk question and to any make-up-your-own prompt. The Investigation first step is take-home (or the opener of the next lesson): tell the group so at the end of the talk time. Talk-time rules: say "You may say pass." Ask for VOLUNTEERS first, then invite others only if they want to. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and no "who got it right?" hands. Talk time: 30 seconds of silent thinking, 2 minutes pairs talk, 1 and a half minutes volunteers share, then tell everyone that the first step of the Investigation (the page after workbook page 2) is take-home, or the opener of the next lesson. Pass is always allowed.

p5l9-exit.note: Minutes 80 to 85.5. Answers: (a) 82 (dots = 4 × figure number + 2; 4 × 20 + 2 = 82, or 6 + 19 × 4). (b) Figure 25 (102 − 2 = 100, 100 ÷ 4 = 25). Extension: a square grid of matchsticks: 1 by 1 uses 4 sticks, 2 by 2 uses 12. How many for 3 by 3 and 10 by 10? (24 and 220.)

p5l9-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 85.5 to 88. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new.
